title: Context-Free Grammars & Pushdown Automata
summary: Grammars, derivations, and pushdown automata as the machine model — the theory behind parsers.

slides.subTitle: Productions and derivations
slides.markdown:
A **context-free grammar (CFG)** is a set of **production rules** rewriting non-terminal symbols into sequences of terminals and non-terminals, e.g. `S -> A + A`, `A -> "a"`.

A **derivation** applies rules repeatedly, starting from the start symbol `S`, until only terminals remain — that sequence of terminals is a string in the language.

![A parse tree built from CFG productions](assets/cfg-parse-tree.svg)

assets.alt: A parse tree built from CFG productions

slides.subTitle: Parse trees and ambiguity
slides.markdown:
A **parse tree** shows how a string was derived — each internal node is a production applied. A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string has *more than one* valid parse tree.

Ambiguity is a real practical problem: `1 + 2 * 3` parsed one way gives `(1+2)*3 = 9`, parsed another gives `1+(2*3) = 7`. A grammar for arithmetic must be designed (with precedence levels as separate non-terminals) to rule out the wrong tree.

Compilers care a lot about this — an ambiguous grammar makes "what does this code mean" genuinely undefined until resolved.

slides.subTitle: Pushdown automata
slides.markdown:
A **pushdown automaton (PDA)** is a finite automaton plus one **stack** — unbounded memory, but only accessible last-in-first-out.

That single addition is exactly what lets it track nesting depth a DFA can't: push on an open bracket, pop on a close, and check the stack is empty at the end.

![A pushdown automaton's finite control and stack](assets/pda-stack.svg)

assets.alt: A pushdown automaton's finite control and stack

slides.subTitle: CFG ↔ PDA equivalence
slides.markdown:
Just as regular languages ↔ finite automata, **context-free languages ↔ pushdown automata**: every CFG has an equivalent PDA that accepts exactly the strings it derives, and vice versa.

You don't need the full construction proof to use this — the practical takeaway is that "can I write a grammar for it" and "can a stack-based machine recognize it" are the same question, asked two different ways.

This equivalence is why real parsers (which are essentially PDAs) are built directly from a grammar specification.

slides.subTitle: The Chomsky hierarchy
slides.markdown:
The **Chomsky hierarchy** ranks language classes by machinery needed: **regular** ⊂ **context-free** ⊂ **context-sensitive** ⊂ **recursively enumerable**. Each ring strictly contains the previous.

![The Chomsky hierarchy as nested language classes](assets/chomsky-hierarchy.svg)

Most programming syntax lives at the context-free level; a full Turing machine is needed only for the outermost class.

assets.alt: The Chomsky hierarchy as nested language classes

slides.subTitle: Top-down vs bottom-up
slides.markdown:
Real parsers implement CFG recognition two ways.

| | Top-down | Bottom-up |
|---|---|---|
| Builds tree | Root to leaves | Leaves to root |
| Example | Recursive descent | LR/LALR (yacc/bison) |
| Handles left recursion | Poorly (needs rewriting) | Naturally |
| Ease of hand-writing | Easy to write and debug | Usually generated by a tool |

Decide by tooling and grammar shape: hand-written recursive descent for simple/DSL grammars, generated LR parsers for full language grammars with complex precedence. (Area 6 `compilers` covers parser implementation in depth.)

Not every useful language is context-free. The classic example: `{aⁿbⁿcⁿ}` — equal counts of `a`, `b`, `c` in that order. A PDA's single stack can match two counts against each other (push `a`s, pop on `b`s) but can't simultaneously check a *third* count against the same stack.

This matters practically: checking that a variable is declared before every use (across a whole program) is a **context-sensitive** property — grammars alone can enforce syntax, but semantic checks like this need extra machinery (symbol tables, separate passes) beyond the parser.

slides.subTitle: Not everything a parser needs is context-free
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to assume "if I can write a grammar for the syntax, the parser handles everything." In practice, real languages have rules a CFG can't express: type checking, matching variable declarations to uses, or ensuring function arity matches a call site.

These are **context-sensitive** constraints, handled in a separate **semantic analysis** pass after parsing — not baked into the grammar.

Don't try to force these checks into the grammar itself; it's the wrong tool, and real compilers deliberately split "is this syntactically valid" from "does this actually make sense."
